dx: Squamous cell carcinoma of the penis in an uncircumcised man with phimosis and recurrent balanitis
case: A 66-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of a foul-smelling discharge and a lump under his foreskin. He is uncircumcised. For the past 8 years his foreskin could not be retracted, after many episodes of inflammation of the glans. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus with a hemoglobin A1c of 9.4% (normal below 5.7%) and has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 45 years. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a scarred, nonretractable prepuce. After a dorsal slit, a 2.5-cm ulcerated, exophytic mass is seen on the glans. A firm, nontender 2-cm left inguinal lymph node is palpable. Biopsy shows invasive keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma. In situ hybridization of the tumor is positive for HPV 16. Diagnosis: squamous cell carcinoma of the penis.

questions.stem: Ten years earlier, a sharply demarcated, shiny red, velvety plaque was noted on his glans. It persisted for 2 years despite topical antifungal treatment and was never biopsied. Which of the following histologic findings would that plaque most likely have shown?
options: Papillary squamous proliferation with koilocytes and no atypia
Homogenized dermal collagen beneath a band of lymphocytes
Full-thickness squamous atypia above an intact basement membrane
Pseudohyphae and neutrophils within the superficial keratin layer
approach: Link the clues: a persistent red velvety plaque on the glans of an uncircumcised older man is erythroplasia of Queyrat.
Recall that erythroplasia of Queyrat, Bowen disease (shaft), and bowenoid papulosis are forms of squamous cell carcinoma in situ.
Carcinoma in situ means atypical cells through the full thickness of the epithelium with no breach of the basement membrane.
questions.why: Erythroplasia of Queyrat is squamous cell carcinoma in situ of the glans or inner prepuce. It looks like a shiny red, velvety plaque and does not respond to antifungals. Bowen disease is the same lesion on the shaft or scrotum, and bowenoid papulosis is multiple small papules in younger men that rarely progress. Untreated, the in situ lesion can become invasive carcinoma. High-risk HPV (especially type 16), lack of circumcision, phimosis with trapped smegma and chronic inflammation, and smoking all raise the risk.
whyNot: Papillary squamous growth with koilocytes and no atypia describes condyloma acuminatum, caused by low-risk HPV 6 and 11. It is a warty, cauliflower-like growth, not a flat red plaque.

Homogenized dermal collagen under a lymphocytic band is lichen sclerosus (balanitis xerotica obliterans). It produces white, atrophic plaques and can scar the foreskin, but it is not a red velvety plaque.
Correct.
Pseudohyphae with neutrophils in the keratin layer are seen in candidal balanitis. That infection improves with antifungal treatment, which this plaque did not.

topics: Penile carcinoma in situ: erythroplasia of Queyrat, Bowen disease, bowenoid papulosis
Risk factors for penile squamous cell carcinoma

questions.stem: Nine years ago, before the foreskin scarred completely, a urinary catheter was placed during hip surgery. The narrowed foreskin was pulled back for the procedure and left behind the glans. Within hours, the glans became swollen and painful and the foreskin could not be returned to its normal position. Which of the following best explains the swelling of the glans at that time?
options: Tight preputial ring proximal to the corona obstructing venous and lymphatic return
Thrombosis of the superficial dorsal vein of the penis along the shaft
Rupture of the tunica albuginea surrounding the corpora cavernosa
Ballooning of the prepuce from urine trapped behind a pinhole preputial orifice on voiding
approach: A foreskin that is retracted and then cannot be brought forward is paraphimosis, not phimosis.
The narrow ring of foreskin sits behind the corona and acts like a tourniquet on the glans and distal prepuce.
Venous and lymphatic outflow is blocked first, so the tissue swells, and the swelling tightens the ring further.
questions.why: Paraphimosis happens when a tight foreskin is retracted behind the glans and stays there. The constricting band at the coronal sulcus blocks venous and lymphatic drainage of the glans and distal prepuce, which causes edema. Edema makes the ring tighter, and if it is not reduced, arterial inflow can fail and the glans can become ischemic. Phimosis is the opposite problem: a foreskin that cannot be retracted over the glans. A partly narrowed foreskin, as he had then, is the usual setting for paraphimosis.
whyNot: Correct.
Thrombosis of the superficial dorsal vein (Mondor disease of the penis) causes a tender cord along the shaft. It does not trap the foreskin or swell the glans.
Rupture of the tunica albuginea is penile fracture. It follows blunt trauma to an erect penis, with a snap, rapid detumescence, and a shaft hematoma.

Ballooning of the foreskin while voiding happens in phimosis, when urine is trapped behind a pinhole opening with the foreskin forward. It swells the prepuce, not the glans, and does not follow retraction of the foreskin.

topics: Venous and lymphatic drainage of the glans

questions.stem: His earlier episodes of inflammation of the glans caused itching, redness, white curdlike material under the foreskin, and small red satellite papules. Each episode resolved with topical treatment. Which of the following was the most likely cause of these episodes?
options: Herpes simplex virus type 2
Treponema pallidum
Haemophilus ducreyi
Candida albicans
approach: Identify recurrent balanitis in a man with an uncircumcised, poorly retractable foreskin and poorly controlled diabetes.
Match the lesion: itching, white curdlike material, and satellite papules are the pattern of a yeast infection.
Explain the risk: the warm, moist space under the foreskin and glucose-rich urine favor Candida growth.
questions.why: Balanitis is inflammation of the glans and is most often caused by Candida albicans or bacteria. Risk factors are an uncircumcised foreskin, poor hygiene, and diabetes mellitus, all of which he has. Glucose in urine and secretions feeds yeast trapped in the moist preputial space. Candidal balanitis gives a red, itchy glans with white material and satellite papules. Repeated balanitis scars the foreskin and is a common cause of acquired phimosis, which in turn keeps the space closed and makes the next episode more likely.
whyNot: Herpes simplex virus type 2 causes painful grouped vesicles that break into shallow ulcers. It does not cause white curdlike material or satellite papules.
Treponema pallidum causes a single painless, indurated chancre in primary syphilis. It is not itchy and does not recur in this pattern.
Haemophilus ducreyi causes chancroid, a painful ulcer with a ragged undermined border and tender inguinal nodes.
Correct.

topics: Causes and risk factors of balanitis

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man seen in the same clinic reports 8 months of painful erections with an upward bend of the penis. He also has a flexion contracture of the ring finger from Dupuytren disease. Examination of the flaccid penis shows a firm, nontender, 1.5-cm plaque on the dorsal shaft. The glans and foreskin are normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his penile curvature?
options: Diffuse fibrosis of the cavernosal smooth muscle after prolonged ischemia
Localized fibrous plaque within the tunica albuginea
Infiltrating squamous cell carcinoma extending into the corpus spongiosum
Thrombosis of the superficial dorsal vein with surrounding inflammation
approach: Note the triad: a palpable plaque, curvature on erection, and pain, in a man who also has Dupuytren contracture.
Recall that Peyronie disease is a fibrous plaque in the tunica albuginea, a fibroproliferative disorder like Dupuytren disease.
The plaque does not stretch during erection, so the penis bends toward the plaque, here upward from a dorsal plaque.
questions.why: Peyronie disease is a localized fibrous plaque in the tunica albuginea, the tough sheath around the corpora cavernosa. It is thought to follow repeated microtrauma with abnormal wound healing, and it is linked to Dupuytren contracture. Because the plaque cannot stretch, the erect penis curves toward it, and erections can be painful in the early phase. The glans and foreskin are normal, which separates it from penile cancer.
whyNot: Diffuse cavernosal fibrosis after prolonged ischemic priapism causes poor erections and a firm, shortened penis. It is not a single dorsal plaque with curvature.
Correct.
Penile squamous cell carcinoma usually starts on the glans or inner prepuce as a visible mass or ulcer. His glans and foreskin are normal.
Superficial dorsal vein thrombosis (penile Mondor disease) causes a tender cord in the skin of the shaft. It does not involve the tunica albuginea or bend the erect penis.

dx: Erectile dysfunction after ischemic priapism in sickle cell disease
case: A 24-year-old man with sickle cell disease (hemoglobin SS) comes to the physician because of 4 years of erections too weak for intercourse. At age 20, he had a painful erection that lasted 30 hours before he sought care; it was treated by aspiration and irrigation of the corpora cavernosa. Since then he has had no morning erections. Libido, orgasm, and ejaculation are preserved. He takes hydroxyurea and folic acid. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg. The penile shaft is firm and shortened with no discrete plaque. Testes are normal in size. Perineal sensation, the bulbocavernosus reflex, and lower limb reflexes are normal. Serum total testosterone is 540 ng/dL (normal 300 to 1,000). Nocturnal penile tumescence testing shows no erections during sleep. Diagnosis: erectile dysfunction after ischemic priapism.

questions.stem: His physician explains why the sleep study was ordered. Which of the following findings on that study would have most strongly indicated a psychogenic cause of his erectile dysfunction?
options: Normal rigid erections occurring during REM sleep
Absent erections during both REM and non-REM sleep
Brief partial erections that quickly lose rigidity
Erections only after a phosphodiesterase inhibitor dose
approach: Recall that erections during REM sleep happen automatically and need intact nerves, arterial inflow, and functioning cavernosal tissue.
If those sleep erections are normal, the hardware works, so a failure during sexual activity points to a psychogenic cause.
Absent or poor sleep erections point to an organic cause: vascular, neurogenic, endocrine, drug-induced, or structural, as in this patient.
questions.why: Erectile dysfunction is classified as vascular (atherosclerosis), neurogenic (diabetes, spinal cord injury, pelvic surgery), endocrine (hypogonadism, hyperprolactinemia), drug-induced, or psychogenic. Several erections occur during REM sleep each night without any sexual thought. Normal nocturnal erections show that nerves, blood supply, and erectile tissue all work, which points to a psychogenic cause. His absent nocturnal erections, normal testosterone, and normal neurologic examination fit an organic cause in the erectile tissue itself.
whyNot: Correct.
Absent sleep erections, as in this patient, indicate an organic cause rather than a psychogenic one.
Erections that start but cannot be held point toward venous leak or structural damage to the cavernosal tissue, an organic cause.
A response to a phosphodiesterase inhibitor shows that some nitric oxide signaling and tissue function remain. It does not separate psychogenic from organic causes.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why the 30-hour delay before treatment of his priapism led to permanent erectile dysfunction?
options: Compression injury of the cavernous nerves by the engorged corpora
Infarction of the testes with loss of Leydig cell testosterone
Hypoxic, acidotic stasis causing smooth muscle fibrosis
Unregulated arterial inflow from a ruptured cavernosal artery
approach: Recognize ischemic (low-flow) priapism: a painful erection over 4 hours in a patient with sickle cell disease.
Sickled red cells block venous outflow from the corpora, so blood stagnates and becomes hypoxic and acidotic.
After many hours, the trabecular smooth muscle dies and is replaced by fibrous tissue, which cannot relax to make an erection.
questions.why: Ischemic priapism is a compartment-syndrome-like state of the penis. In sickle cell disease, sickled cells obstruct venous drainage, so trapped blood loses oxygen and becomes acidotic, which causes pain. Smooth muscle injury begins within hours, and by about 24 to 48 hours, necrosis and fibrosis are likely. Fibrotic corpora cannot relax or compress the draining veins, which explains his permanent erectile dysfunction. Drugs that cause ischemic priapism include trazodone, alpha blockers, and injected vasoactive agents.
whyNot: The injury in ischemic priapism comes from hypoxia and acidosis in the trapped blood, which damages the cavernosal smooth muscle. Compression of the cavernous nerves is not the mechanism.
Sickle cell disease can cause testicular infarction, but his testes are normal in size and his testosterone is normal.
Correct.

Unregulated arterial inflow from a ruptured cavernosal artery causes high-flow (nonischemic) priapism, usually after perineal trauma. It is painless, the blood is well oxygenated, and fibrosis is uncommon.

questions.stem: He is given a phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor, which increases cGMP in cavernosal smooth muscle, but his erections do not improve. Which of the following best explains the poor response?
options: Absent nitric oxide release from the cavernous nerves
Inadequate testosterone support of nitric oxide synthase
Excess sympathetic outflow from performance anxiety
Loss of smooth muscle that relaxes to compress venules
approach: Lay out the normal chain: nitric oxide raises cGMP, cGMP relaxes cavernosal smooth muscle, arterial blood fills the sinusoids, and the expanding sinusoids press the subtunical venules against the tunica albuginea.
A PDE5 inhibitor only prolongs cGMP, so it works only if the smooth muscle can still respond.
His nerves and testosterone are normal, so the failure lies in fibrotic tissue that cannot relax or trap blood.
questions.why: Erection starts when parasympathetic nerves and endothelium release nitric oxide. Nitric oxide activates guanylyl cyclase, cGMP rises, and cavernosal smooth muscle relaxes. Arterial inflow fills the sinusoids, which expand and squeeze the small draining veins against the stiff tunica albuginea, trapping blood. PDE5 inhibitors block cGMP breakdown, but they cannot help when the smooth muscle has been replaced by fibrous tissue. Without relaxing, expanding sinusoids, veno-occlusion fails.
whyNot: Loss of nitric oxide release from damaged cavernous nerves causes neurogenic erectile dysfunction, as after radical prostatectomy. His sensation and reflexes are normal.
Testosterone supports libido and nitric oxide synthase expression, but his testosterone level is normal.
Performance anxiety raises sympathetic tone and is a psychogenic cause. He has no nocturnal erections, which points to an organic cause.
Correct.

topics: Nitric oxide and cGMP in erection

questions.stem: Rhythmic contraction of the bulbospongiosus and ischiocavernosus muscles expels semen during his ejaculation, which remains normal. These contractions depend on which of the following nerves?
options: Pelvic splanchnic nerves
Pudendal nerve
Hypogastric nerves
Genitofemoral nerve
approach: Separate the three phases: erection, emission, and ejaculation.
Erection is parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnic, S2 to S4), and emission into the posterior urethra is sympathetic (hypogastric).
Expulsion by skeletal perineal muscles is somatic, carried by the pudendal nerve.
questions.why: The bulbospongiosus and ischiocavernosus are skeletal muscles of the perineum, so they get somatic motor fibers from the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4). Their rhythmic contractions expel semen from the urethra. Emission, the movement of sperm and gland secretions into the posterior urethra, is sympathetic through the hypogastric nerves. Erection is parasympathetic through the pelvic splanchnic nerves. His preserved ejaculation fits a tissue problem, not a nerve problem.
whyNot: The pelvic splanchnic nerves carry parasympathetic fibers (S2 to S4) that cause erection by releasing nitric oxide. They do not drive skeletal muscle.
Correct.
The hypogastric nerves carry sympathetic fibers that cause emission: contraction of the vas deferens, seminal vesicles, and prostate, and closure of the internal urethral sphincter.
The genitofemoral nerve supplies the cremaster muscle and skin of the anterior scrotum and upper thigh. It is the efferent limb of the cremasteric reflex.

topics: Innervation of erection, emission, and ejaculation

case: A 19-year-old man comes to the emergency department 6 hours after a lacrosse ball struck his scrotum during a game. He has had aching right scrotal pain and swelling since the injury. Temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Examination shows bruising of the right scrotal skin and a tense, tender right hemiscrotum. The testis cannot be palpated separately from the swelling, and its lie cannot be judged. The mass does not transilluminate. The right cremasteric reflex is present. Doppler ultrasonography shows a complex fluid collection with internal echoes surrounding an intact right testis with normal blood flow. Urinalysis is normal. Diagnosis: traumatic hematocele.

questions.stem: On ultrasonography, the collection lies against the front and sides of the testis but not its posterior border, where the epididymis attaches. In which of the following spaces has the blood most likely collected?
options: Beneath the tunica albuginea in the testicular parenchyma
Within the dartos layer of the scrotal wall
Between the external and internal spermatic fasciae
Between the two layers of the tunica vaginalis
approach: Note the shape of the collection: it covers the front and sides of the testis but spares the back, where the epididymis attaches.
Recall that the tunica vaginalis has this shape, because it is a closed serous sac that covers the testis except along its posterior border.
Blood in the tunica vaginalis is a hematocele, which fits the trauma, the internal echoes, and the lack of transillumination.
questions.why: The tunica vaginalis is the closed lower end of the processus vaginalis. Its visceral layer covers the front and sides of the testis, and its parietal layer lines the inner scrotal wall, with a thin potential space between them. The posterior border of the testis, where the epididymis and vessels attach, is left uncovered, so fluid in this sac wraps around the front and sides only. Blood in this space is a hematocele, and serous fluid in the same space is a hydrocele. Blood blocks light, so a hematocele does not transilluminate, while a hydrocele glows.
whyNot: Blood beneath the tunica albuginea is an intratesticular hematoma, inside the testis itself. His testis is intact on ultrasound, and the collection surrounds it from outside.
Bleeding into the dartos layer is a scrotal wall hematoma, which thickens and bruises the skin. It does not form a collection wrapped around the testis that spares its posterior border.
Blood between the spermatic fasciae spreads through the coverings of the cord and testis. It is not held against the front and sides of the testis by a closed serous sac.
Correct.

topics: Layers of the scrotum and the tunica vaginalis

questions.stem: His 6-month-old nephew has a soft, nontender right scrotal swelling that transilluminates. His mother reports that it is larger in the evening and after crying and smaller in the morning. Persistence of which of the following embryologic structures best explains the nephew's swelling?
options: Gubernaculum
Processus vaginalis
Urachus
Mesonephric (Wolffian) duct
approach: A transilluminating fluid collection around the testis is a hydrocele.
A size that changes with activity and time of day means the fluid moves to and from the peritoneal cavity: a communicating hydrocele.
That connection is a processus vaginalis that failed to close.
questions.why: The processus vaginalis is an outpouching of peritoneum that leads the testis into the scrotum. Normally it closes, and only its lower part stays as the tunica vaginalis. If it stays open, peritoneal fluid flows into the scrotum and back, so the swelling changes in size: a communicating hydrocele. A wide opening can let bowel through as an indirect inguinal hernia. A noncommunicating hydrocele has a closed processus and a fixed size, and in adults it may follow infection, trauma, or a tumor.
whyNot: The gubernaculum guides testicular descent and becomes the scrotal ligament. It is a fibrous cord and does not carry fluid.
Correct.
A patent urachus connects the bladder to the umbilicus and leaks urine from the umbilicus. It does not reach the scrotum.
The mesonephric duct forms the epididymis, vas deferens, and seminal vesicle. It does not link the scrotum to the peritoneal cavity.

questions.stem: Before ultrasonography, his physician considered testicular torsion triggered by the injury. Which of the following findings in this patient most strongly argued against torsion?
options: Pain that began during vigorous physical activity
Swelling that did not transilluminate
Intact ipsilateral cremasteric reflex
Tachycardia with a pulse of 92/min
approach: Recall the torsion picture: sudden severe pain, a high-riding testis often lying horizontally, and an absent cremasteric reflex.
The cremasteric reflex is absent in almost all cases of torsion.
A preserved reflex makes torsion much less likely, though ultrasound with Doppler is still needed.
questions.why: Testicular torsion is twisting of the spermatic cord, usually in a testis with a bell-clapper deformity that lets it rotate freely. The thin-walled veins close first, so the testis swells and becomes congested; then arterial inflow stops and the testis infarcts within hours. Typical findings are sudden severe pain, a high-riding testis, and an absent cremasteric reflex. A present cremasteric reflex is the single exam finding that argues most against torsion. His ultrasound later confirmed normal blood flow.
whyNot: Torsion often starts during exercise or sleep, and trauma can trigger it, so pain beginning with activity does not exclude it.
Failure to transilluminate fits blood or a solid mass. It does not separate torsion from a hematocele.
Correct.
A fast pulse reflects pain and stress from any scrotal emergency. It does not help separate torsion from other causes.

questions.stem: Six weeks later, after the hematocele resolves, follow-up ultrasonography shows a 1.5-cm solid hypoechoic mass within the right testis. He has developed tender bilateral breast enlargement. Serum estradiol is increased, and serum alpha-fetoprotein and beta-hCG are within the reference ranges. Orchiectomy shows sheets of large polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and rod-shaped cytoplasmic crystals. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Leydig cell tumor
Classic seminoma
Choriocarcinoma
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
approach: Gynecomastia with a testicular mass means the tumor is making estrogen, making androgen that is aromatized, or making hCG.
A normal beta-hCG removes choriocarcinoma, and a normal alpha-fetoprotein argues against yolk sac elements.
Polygonal eosinophilic cells with rod-shaped crystals (Reinke crystals) identify a Leydig cell tumor.
questions.why: Leydig cell tumors are sex cord-stromal tumors that can secrete androgens, estrogens, or both. In adults, estrogen excess causes gynecomastia and reduced libido; in boys, androgen excess causes precocious puberty. Histology shows large polygonal cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, and about a quarter to a third contain Reinke crystals. Most are benign. Testicular tumors are one reason a hematocele can appear with little trauma, so a mass found after the blood clears must be evaluated.
whyNot: Correct.
Classic seminoma has sheets of clear cells with lymphocytes in fibrous septa. It does not usually make hormones that cause gynecomastia.
Choriocarcinoma can cause gynecomastia through very high hCG levels. His beta-hCG is normal, and the tumor would show cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast.
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common testicular tumor in men over 60. It is often bilateral, has sheets of atypical lymphoid cells, and does not secrete estrogen.

dx: Left varicocele with a coexisting spermatocele in an infertile man
case: A 29-year-old man comes to the physician because he and his partner have not conceived after 18 months of regular unprotected intercourse. Her evaluation is normal. He reports a dull ache in the left scrotum after standing for long periods. Examination while standing shows a soft mass above the left testis that feels like a bag of worms, enlarges with a Valsalva maneuver, and empties when he lies supine. It does not transilluminate. A separate 1.5-cm smooth, nontender cyst sits at the head of the right epididymis, above and apart from the right testis, and transilluminates. The left testis measures 13 mL and the right 19 mL (normal 15 to 25). Semen analysis shows a sperm concentration of 9 million/mL (reference 15 million/mL or more), 24% progressive motility (reference 32% or more), and 2% normal forms (reference 4% or more). Diagnosis: left varicocele and right spermatocele.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains his reduced sperm production?
options: Obstruction of sperm transport by the epididymal cyst
Heat injury to germ cells from poor countercurrent cooling
Suppression of FSH by excess testosterone from the left testis
Antisperm antibodies formed after rupture of the epididymal cyst
approach: Identify the varicocele: a bag of worms above the testis that fills on standing and empties on lying down.
Normally, cool venous blood in the pampiniform plexus cools incoming arterial blood, keeping the testis about 2 to 3 °C (3.6 to 5.4 °F) below core temperature.
Pooled warm blood in dilated veins blunts this exchange, and heat impairs spermatogenesis, which fits his smaller left testis and abnormal semen.
questions.why: A varicocele is dilation of the pampiniform plexus. The plexus normally wraps around the testicular artery and acts as a countercurrent heat exchanger. When the veins are dilated and blood pools, the testis runs warmer, and heat harms developing germ cells. The result is lower sperm count, poor motility, abnormal shapes, and over time a smaller testis. Varicocele is the most common correctable cause of male infertility. A new left varicocele in an older man, especially one that does not empty when lying down, should raise concern for renal cell carcinoma blocking the left renal vein.
whyNot: A spermatocele usually does not block sperm transport, and his is on the right while the testicular damage is on the left.
Correct.
A varicocele does not raise testosterone. Damage to Sertoli cells and germ cells tends to raise FSH, not suppress it.
Spermatoceles rarely rupture, and nothing suggests a rupture here. Antisperm antibodies are more typical after vasectomy, trauma, or orchitis.

topics: Countercurrent heat exchange in the spermatic cord

questions.stem: The right epididymal cyst is aspirated during later surgery. Which of the following findings would identify it as a spermatocele rather than a simple epididymal cyst?
options: Transmission of light through the mass
Location separate from the testis
Smooth wall lined by cuboidal cells
Milky fluid containing spermatozoa
approach: Both a spermatocele and a simple epididymal cyst are smooth, transilluminating masses separate from the testis.
A spermatocele is a dilated part of the epididymal duct system, so its fluid contains sperm.
A simple epididymal cyst holds clear fluid without sperm.
questions.why: A spermatocele is a cystic dilation of the epididymis, usually at the head, that contains sperm. On exam it is smooth, sits above and separate from the testis, and transilluminates. An epididymal cyst looks and feels the same but holds clear serous fluid without sperm. Aspirated spermatocele fluid is usually milky or cloudy and shows spermatozoa under the microscope. Both are benign and usually do not cause infertility.
whyNot: Both spermatoceles and simple epididymal cysts contain fluid that lets light through, so transillumination does not separate them.
Both lesions arise from the epididymis and are felt apart from the testis. Separation from the testis mainly distinguishes them from a testicular tumor.
Both cysts have a smooth wall with a simple cuboidal to columnar epithelial lining, so the lining does not separate them.
Correct.

questions.stem: He asks why the dilated veins are only on the left side. Which of the following venous drainage patterns best explains this?
options: Left testicular vein entering the left renal vein at a right angle
Left testicular vein entering the inferior vena cava at an acute angle
Right testicular vein entering the right renal vein at a right angle
Left testicular vein entering the left common iliac vein directly
approach: Trace the arteries: both testicular arteries arise from the abdominal aorta just below the renal arteries.
Trace the veins: the right testicular vein enters the inferior vena cava at an acute angle, and the left enters the left renal vein at a right angle.
The left vein is longer, meets higher pressure, and the left renal vein can be compressed between the superior mesenteric artery and aorta, so left varicoceles are far more common.
questions.why: The testicular arteries come from the abdominal aorta, but the veins drain asymmetrically. The right testicular vein empties obliquely into the inferior vena cava. The left testicular vein runs a longer course and joins the left renal vein at a right angle, where pressure is higher and flow is less favorable. The left renal vein also passes between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta and can be compressed there. These features raise pressure in the left pampiniform plexus, so about 85 to 90% of varicoceles are on the left. A tumor in the left renal vein can cause a new left varicocele.
whyNot: Correct.
The left testicular vein does not drain into the inferior vena cava. It is the right testicular vein that enters the inferior vena cava at an acute angle.

The right testicular vein normally drains into the inferior vena cava, not the right renal vein. An isolated right varicocele is uncommon and should prompt a search for a retroperitoneal mass or other venous obstruction.
The testicular veins do not drain into the common iliac veins. They ascend on the posterior abdominal wall to the renal vein level.

questions.stem: Further morphology testing shows that many spermatozoa have round heads that lack the cap covering the anterior two-thirds of the nucleus. Which organelle of the developing spermatid normally forms this missing structure?
options: Distal centriole
Mitochondria
Golgi apparatus
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
approach: Name the missing cap: the acrosome, which covers the front of the sperm nucleus and holds enzymes.
In spermiogenesis, the acrosome forms from Golgi vesicles that fuse over the nucleus.
Without an acrosome, the sperm cannot complete the acrosome reaction needed to get through the zona pellucida.
questions.why: Spermiogenesis turns a round spermatid into a spermatozoon. The Golgi apparatus makes the acrosome, a cap of hydrolytic enzymes over the nucleus. A centriole forms the axoneme of the flagellum, mitochondria pack into the midpiece, and most cytoplasm is shed as a residual body. After ejaculation, sperm undergo capacitation in the female tract, which changes the membrane and allows the acrosome reaction at the zona pellucida. Sperm without an acrosome cannot penetrate the zona and cannot fertilize the egg naturally.
whyNot: The distal centriole gives rise to the axoneme of the flagellum, which makes the sperm motile. It does not form the head cap.
Mitochondria wrap around the midpiece and supply ATP for flagellar movement. They do not form the acrosome.
Correct.
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum makes steroids and lipids in Leydig cells. It does not form the acrosome in spermatids.

case: A 26-year-old man comes to the physician because he and his partner have not conceived after 2 years of trying. Five years earlier, during a campus outbreak, he had fever and swelling of both parotid glands, followed 6 days later by painful swelling of both testes. He had never been vaccinated. Physical examination shows normal virilization and no gynecomastia. Both testes are small and soft, each about 8 mL (normal 15 to 25). Laboratory studies show FSH 28 mIU/mL (normal 1.5 to 12.4), LH 9.8 mIU/mL (normal 1.7 to 8.6), and total testosterone 340 ng/dL (normal 300 to 1,000). Semen analysis shows a normal volume with a sperm concentration of 2 million/mL (reference 15 million/mL or more). Karyotype is 46,XY. Diagnosis: testicular atrophy after bilateral mumps orchitis.

questions.stem: During the same outbreak, his 22-year-old roommate, who is sexually active, developed acute pain and swelling of the right scrotum with dysuria and a scant mucoid urethral discharge. He had no parotid swelling. The tender swelling began at the back of the testis, and pain eased when the scrotum was elevated. Which of the following was the most likely cause of the roommate's illness?
options: Mumps virus
Escherichia coli
Chlamydia trachomatis
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
approach: Separate the two pictures: mumps orchitis follows parotitis and involves the testis itself, while epididymo-orchitis starts in the epididymis behind the testis.
Urethritis with dysuria and discharge in a sexually active young man points to a sexually transmitted cause.
In men under about 35, Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae cause most epididymitis; in older men, coliforms such as E. coli do.
questions.why: Epididymo-orchitis in sexually active young men usually ascends from urethritis caused by C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae. The epididymis at the back of the testis is tender, and lifting the scrotum often eases pain. A scant mucoid discharge fits chlamydia. In older men, E. coli and other coliforms from urinary tract infection or prostate obstruction are the usual cause. Mumps orchitis is a viral infection of the testis itself, usually about a week after parotitis in a postpubertal male. It can lead to atrophy and infertility, as in this patient.
whyNot: Mumps orchitis follows parotitis and affects the testis directly. The roommate had no parotid swelling and had urethritis.

Escherichia coli causes epididymitis mainly in older men with urinary tract infection or outlet obstruction, or in men who have anal intercourse. A young man with urethral discharge more likely has a sexually transmitted cause.
Correct.
Tuberculous epididymitis develops slowly with a firm, beaded epididymis and sterile pyuria. It is not an acute illness with urethral discharge.

questions.stem: Male infertility is classified as pretesticular, testicular, or post-testicular. Which of the following causes of infertility belongs to the same category as his condition?
options: Kallmann syndrome
Hyperprolactinemia
Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
Cryptorchidism
approach: Use the gonadotropins to locate the problem: high FSH and LH with small testes mean the testis itself has failed.
Pretesticular causes have low gonadotropins, and post-testicular causes have normal testes and hormones with blocked outflow.
Testicular causes include Klinefelter syndrome, cryptorchidism, varicocele, and mumps orchitis.
questions.why: Male infertility is grouped by where the problem lies. Pretesticular causes are hormonal, such as hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from Kallmann syndrome or hyperprolactinemia, with low LH and FSH. Testicular causes damage sperm production directly: Klinefelter syndrome, cryptorchidism, varicocele, toxins, and mumps orchitis. They raise FSH as feedback is lost. Post-testicular causes block sperm transport, such as congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens in cystic fibrosis, which gives a low semen volume with normal testes. His high FSH, small testes, and normal semen volume place him in the testicular group.
whyNot: Kallmann syndrome is a pretesticular cause. Absent GnRH makes LH and FSH low, while his are high.
Hyperprolactinemia is a pretesticular cause. It suppresses GnRH and lowers LH and FSH, while his are high.
Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens is a post-testicular cause, with normal testes, normal FSH, and a low semen volume. His testes are atrophic and his semen volume is normal.
Correct.

topics: Interpreting FSH and LH in men

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why his FSH is raised more than his LH?
options: Reduced testosterone secretion by Leydig cells
Reduced inhibin B secretion by Sertoli cells
Reduced androgen-binding protein from Sertoli cells
Increased estradiol from peripheral aromatization
approach: Recall the two arms: LH drives Leydig cell testosterone, and FSH drives Sertoli cells, which support sperm and make androgen-binding protein and inhibin B.
Testosterone feeds back mainly on LH, and inhibin B feeds back selectively on FSH.
His germ cells and Sertoli cell function are badly damaged while testosterone is near normal, so FSH rises most.
questions.why: In the male axis, LH stimulates Leydig cells to make testosterone, and FSH stimulates Sertoli cells. Sertoli cells make androgen-binding protein, which keeps testosterone high in the tubules, and inhibin B, which suppresses FSH. Testosterone feeds back on the hypothalamus and pituitary mainly to lower LH. Mumps orchitis destroys seminiferous tubules, so inhibin B falls and FSH rises sharply. Leydig cells are more resistant, so testosterone stays near normal and LH rises only a little.
whyNot: Loss of Leydig cell testosterone would mainly raise LH. His testosterone is in the low-normal range and his LH is only mildly raised.
Correct.
Androgen-binding protein concentrates testosterone in the tubules, but it does not feed back on the pituitary to control FSH.
Raised estradiol would suppress both LH and FSH. It would not explain high gonadotropins.

questions.stem: His semen shows clumped spermatozoa, and IgG and IgA antibodies are found bound to the surface of the few sperm present. Which of the following best explains how these antibodies formed?
options: Disruption of the Sertoli cell barrier exposing sperm antigens
Molecular mimicry between mumps nucleoprotein and sperm antigens
Polyclonal B-cell activation by a mumps virus superantigen
Deficiency of complement regulatory proteins on spermatozoa
approach: Recall that sperm antigens appear at puberty, long after self-tolerance is set, so the immune system treats them as foreign.
Normally they stay hidden behind tight junctions between Sertoli cells (the blood-testis barrier) and local immunosuppression.
Inflammation from orchitis breaks the barrier, exposes sperm antigens, and triggers antisperm antibodies.
questions.why: The testis is an immune-privileged site. Tight junctions between neighboring Sertoli cells form the blood-testis barrier, which hides meiotic and postmeiotic germ cells from the immune system. Local factors, such as regulatory T cells and immunosuppressive cytokines, add protection. Trauma, vasectomy, torsion, or orchitis can break the barrier and expose sperm antigens, leading to antisperm antibodies that clump sperm and block their movement and binding to the egg. Autoimmune orchitis with antibodies against testicular tissue can also cause hypogonadism.
whyNot: Correct.
Molecular mimicry between mumps proteins and sperm antigens is not an established mechanism. The antibodies follow barrier breakdown and exposure of hidden antigens.
Mumps virus does not act as a superantigen. Superantigens, such as staphylococcal toxic shock toxin, activate T cells broadly rather than causing sperm-specific antibodies.
Antisperm antibodies arise from exposure of hidden antigens, not from loss of complement regulators on sperm.

dx: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea in a distance runner
case: A 20-year-old woman who runs collegiate cross-country comes to the physician because she has not had a menstrual period for 7 months. Menarche was at age 13, and her cycles were regular until this season. She now runs about 110 km (68 mi) a week and has lost 6 kg (13 lb). Three months ago she had a stress fracture of the second metatarsal. Temperature is 36.2 °C (97.2 °F), pulse is 48/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. BMI is 17.6 kg/m2. Breast and pubic hair development are normal, and there is no hirsutism or galactorrhea. Serum hCG is negative. Laboratory studies show FSH 2.1 mIU/mL (follicular phase 3.5 to 12.5), LH 1.0 mIU/mL (follicular phase 2.4 to 12.6), estradiol 15 pg/mL (follicular phase 30 to 120), prolactin 9 ng/mL (normal below 25), and TSH 1.8 μU/mL (normal 0.5 to 4.5). Diagnosis: functional hypothalamic amenorrhea.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how her negative energy balance lowered her gonadotropin levels?
options: Low leptin from reduced fat mass decreasing GnRH pulsatility
Raised prolactin from exercise stress inhibiting GnRH release
Raised estradiol from adipose aromatase suppressing the pituitary
Depleted ovarian follicles reducing inhibin and estradiol output
approach: Low FSH, LH, and estradiol with normal prolactin and TSH place the problem in the hypothalamus.
Leptin from fat cells signals energy stores to the hypothalamus, partly through kisspeptin neurons that drive GnRH.
Heavy training with too little intake lowers fat and leptin, so GnRH pulses slow and gonadotropins fall.
questions.why: Leptin is made by adipocytes in proportion to fat mass and signals that energy stores are adequate for reproduction. When intake does not cover the energy cost of training, leptin falls, and kisspeptin and GnRH pulses slow. LH and FSH fall, follicles do not mature, estradiol stays low, and menses stop. Low estrogen speeds bone loss, which explains her stress fracture. High cortisol and low thyroid hormone from energy deficit add to the effect.
whyNot: Correct.
High prolactin can suppress GnRH, but her prolactin is normal.
Her estradiol is low, not high. With a low fat mass, adipose aromatization would also be small.
Follicle depletion is ovarian failure, which raises FSH and LH as feedback is lost. Her gonadotropins are low.

topics: Low energy availability and bone loss

questions.stem: Her physician considers restoring ovulation with an infusion pump that delivers GnRH. Which of the following regimens would produce a sustained rise in her LH and FSH?
options: Continuous infusion, which keeps GnRH receptors occupied and active
Continuous infusion, which increases the number of GnRH receptors
Pulses about every 60 to 90 minutes, keeping receptors responsive
Once-daily large bolus, which reproduces the midcycle LH surge
approach: Recall that the hypothalamus releases GnRH in pulses, roughly every 1 to 2 hours.
Pulses let pituitary GnRH receptors recover between exposures, so gonadotrophs keep releasing LH and FSH.
Continuous GnRH desensitizes and down-regulates the receptors, which suppresses LH and FSH after a brief flare.
questions.why: Gonadotrophs respond to the pattern of GnRH, not just the amount. Pulsatile GnRH keeps receptors sensitive and drives LH and FSH release, and pulse frequency shapes the balance: faster pulses favor LH and slower pulses favor FSH. Continuous exposure causes an initial rise and then receptor desensitization and down-regulation, so gonadotropins fall. That is why long-acting GnRH agonists like leuprolide are used to shut down the axis in prostate cancer, endometriosis, and precocious puberty. A pulsatile pump can restore ovulation in hypothalamic amenorrhea.
whyNot: Continuous GnRH does occupy receptors, but sustained occupancy desensitizes them, so LH and FSH fall after an early flare.
Continuous GnRH lowers receptor number through down-regulation. It does not increase it.
Correct.
A single daily dose is not the physiologic pattern and does not reproduce the midcycle surge, which is triggered by rising estradiol switching to positive feedback.

questions.stem: Her 31-year-old sister has had no menses for 6 months since a dilation and curettage for retained products of conception after a miscarriage. A pregnancy test is negative, and she had no bleeding after a course of estrogen followed by progestin. Which of the following laboratory patterns would be expected in the sister?
options: Decreased FSH and LH, decreased estradiol, normal prolactin
Normal FSH and LH, normal estradiol, normal prolactin
Increased FSH and LH, decreased estradiol, normal prolactin
Decreased FSH and LH, decreased estradiol, increased prolactin
approach: Amenorrhea after curettage with no bleeding even after estrogen and progestin points to a scarred endometrium: Asherman syndrome.
In an outflow tract problem, the hypothalamus, pituitary, and ovaries all work normally.
So FSH, LH, estradiol, and prolactin are all normal, and the defect lies in the uterus.
questions.why: Hormone levels localize amenorrhea. Low FSH and LH with low estradiol point to the hypothalamus or pituitary, as in this runner. High FSH and LH with low estradiol point to the ovary, such as primary ovarian insufficiency. High prolactin points to a prolactinoma or other cause of hyperprolactinemia, and TSH screens for thyroid disease. Normal hormones with no bleeding after estrogen and progestin point to the outflow tract. Asherman syndrome is scarring of the endometrial basal layer, usually after vigorous curettage, and the endometrium cannot respond to hormones.
whyNot: Low FSH, LH, and estradiol with normal prolactin is the pattern of hypothalamic amenorrhea, as in the runner.
Correct.
High FSH and LH with low estradiol shows ovarian failure, such as primary ovarian insufficiency.
Low gonadotropins and estradiol with high prolactin suggest a prolactinoma or other cause of hyperprolactinemia that suppresses GnRH.

questions.stem: Like women with polycystic ovary syndrome, she does not ovulate. Unlike them, she is not at increased risk of endometrial hyperplasia. Which of the following best explains this difference?
options: A persistent corpus luteum supplies protective progesterone
High androgen levels keep her endometrium thin and atrophic
Her endometrium lacks estrogen receptors during amenorrhea
Low estradiol gives little stimulus to endometrial growth
approach: Both conditions are anovulatory, so no corpus luteum forms and no progesterone is made.
In PCOS, estrogen levels stay normal or high, so the endometrium keeps proliferating without progesterone to oppose it.
In hypothalamic amenorrhea, estradiol is low, so the endometrium stays thin and does not grow into hyperplasia.
questions.why: Anovulation means no LH surge and no corpus luteum, so the endometrium never gets the progesterone that turns it secretory and limits growth. Whether this matters depends on estrogen. In PCOS, estrogen keeps stimulating the endometrium, causing irregular heavy bleeding and raising the risk of hyperplasia. In hypothalamic amenorrhea from low energy availability, estrogen is low, so the endometrium is thin and there is no bleeding at all. Her main risk is bone loss rather than hyperplasia.
whyNot: She is anovulatory, so no corpus luteum forms and no progesterone is made.
Her androgens are not raised, and she has no hirsutism. Thin endometrium here comes from low estrogen.
The endometrium keeps its estrogen receptors. The issue is a lack of estrogen, not a lack of receptors.
Correct.

case: A 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because of irregular menses and unwanted hair growth. Since menarche at age 12, she has had 5 or 6 periods a year. She has coarse dark hair on her upper lip, chin, and lower abdomen and acne on her jaw. BMI is 33 kg/m2. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 132/84 mm Hg. Velvety hyperpigmented skin is present on the back of the neck. Serum hCG is negative. Laboratory studies show total testosterone 78 ng/dL (normal 15 to 70), SHBG 16 nmol/L (normal 20 to 130), LH 18 mIU/mL and FSH 5 mIU/mL (follicular phase LH 2.4 to 12.6, FSH 3.5 to 12.5), and fasting glucose 108 mg/dL (normal 70 to 99). DHEA sulfate, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, prolactin, and TSH are normal. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows more than 20 small follicles in each ovary. Diagnosis: polycystic ovary syndrome.

questions.stem: The ovarian follicles on ultrasonography each measure 2 to 9 mm and are arranged around the periphery of enlarged ovaries. Which of the following best explains this appearance?
options: Arrest of antral follicles by androgen excess and low relative FSH
Persistence of one unruptured dominant follicle after a missed LH surge
Luteinization of theca cells by very high concentrations of hCG
Implantation of endometrial glands and stroma on the ovarian surface
approach: Note the raised LH to FSH ratio (18 to 5), the high testosterone, and the insulin resistance.
High LH and high insulin drive theca cells to make androgen, and the relative lack of FSH limits granulosa cell aromatase.
The androgen-rich follicles stop growing before one becomes dominant, so many small follicles line the cortex.
questions.why: In PCOS, high LH pulse frequency raises the LH to FSH ratio, and LH drives theca cells to make androgens. Hyperinsulinemia adds to theca androgen output and lowers SHBG. With relatively low FSH and a high local androgen level, small antral follicles stop developing and none becomes dominant. They pile up under a thickened capsule as many small peripheral cysts, often called a string of pearls. No dominant follicle means no estradiol peak, no LH surge, and no ovulation.
whyNot: Correct.
A single dominant follicle that fails to rupture forms a follicular cyst, usually one cyst of 3 cm or more, not many small ones.
Very high hCG from a molar pregnancy or choriocarcinoma causes theca lutein cysts. Her hCG is negative.
Endometrial tissue on the ovary forms an endometrioma, a single cyst of old blood (chocolate cyst).

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how her raised LH increases ovarian androgen production?
options: Stimulation of granulosa cell aromatase activity
Stimulation of granulosa cell androgen synthesis from cholesterol
Stimulation of zona reticularis androgen synthesis
Stimulation of theca cell androgen synthesis from cholesterol
approach: Apply the two-cell model: theca cells have LH receptors and 17α-hydroxylase, so they make androstenedione from cholesterol.
Granulosa cells have FSH receptors and aromatase, so they convert androgens from the theca into estrogens, but they cannot make androgens themselves.
High LH with relatively low FSH pushes more androgen out of the theca than the granulosa cells can aromatize.
questions.why: In the two-cell model, LH acts on theca cells, which take up cholesterol and make androstenedione. The androgen diffuses to granulosa cells, where FSH-induced aromatase converts it to estrogen. In PCOS, high LH drives theca androgen output, and low relative FSH limits aromatization, so androgens build up. In a normal cycle, a dominant follicle raises estradiol high enough for about 2 days that feedback switches from negative to positive and triggers the LH surge. Women with PCOS rarely reach that point.
whyNot: Granulosa cell aromatase is driven by FSH and converts androgens to estrogens, which lowers androgen. It does not raise androgen production.
Granulosa cells lack 17α-hydroxylase and cannot make androgens from cholesterol. They depend on theca cells for androgen substrate.
The zona reticularis makes DHEA and DHEA sulfate under ACTH control, not LH. Her DHEA sulfate is normal.
Correct.

topics: Positive feedback and the LH surge

questions.stem: Her total testosterone is only mildly raised, yet her hirsutism is marked. Which of the following best explains this?
options: Raised hepatic SHBG synthesis from estrogen excess
Increased aromatization of testosterone to estradiol
Low hepatic SHBG synthesis from hyperinsulinemia
Tight testosterone binding to albumin in the plasma
approach: Recall that most testosterone is bound to SHBG (tightly) or albumin (loosely), and only about 1 to 2% is free.
Free and albumin-bound testosterone reach tissues such as hair follicles.
Insulin resistance, obesity, and androgens lower SHBG, so a larger share of her testosterone is free even when the total is only mildly high.
questions.why: Sex steroids travel bound to SHBG and albumin. SHBG binds testosterone tightly, while albumin binds it loosely, so free plus albumin-bound testosterone is the active fraction. The liver makes SHBG; estrogen and thyroid hormone raise it, while insulin, obesity, and androgens lower it. Her low SHBG means more of her testosterone is free to act on hair follicles. That is why hirsutism can be marked when the total testosterone is only a little high.
whyNot: Estrogen raises SHBG, which would bind more testosterone and lower the free fraction. Her SHBG is low.
Aromatization converts testosterone to estradiol, which would lower androgen effects, not increase them.
Correct.
Albumin binds testosterone weakly, which is why albumin-bound testosterone is counted as available to tissues. Tight albumin binding is not the reason for her hirsutism.

questions.stem: Her theca cells take up most of their cholesterol from circulating LDL by receptor-mediated endocytosis. Which of the following steps limits the rate of LH-stimulated androgen synthesis in these cells?
options: Conversion of pregnenolone to progesterone by 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase
Transfer of cholesterol into mitochondria by StAR protein
Synthesis of mevalonate by HMG-CoA reductase
Conversion of androstenedione to estrone by aromatase
approach: Steroid-making cells in the gonads get most of their cholesterol from LDL, not from making it themselves.
The first enzyme of steroid synthesis, side-chain cleavage, sits on the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Moving cholesterol to that membrane by StAR protein is the slow, hormone-regulated step.
questions.why: Gonadal and placental cells obtain cholesterol mainly from LDL by receptor-mediated endocytosis. LH, acting through cAMP, rapidly raises StAR protein, which carries cholesterol from the outer to the inner mitochondrial membrane. There, side-chain cleavage enzyme converts it to pregnenolone, the start of all steroid hormones. StAR transfer is the rate-limiting step, and mutations in StAR cause congenital lipoid adrenal hyperplasia with failure of adrenal and gonadal steroids.
whyNot: 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase is a later enzyme in the pathway and does not limit the rate of LH-stimulated synthesis.
Correct.
HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis, but theca cells rely mainly on LDL cholesterol rather than making their own.
Aromatase works in granulosa cells and converts androgens to estrogens. It is downstream of androgen synthesis.

topics: LDL as the cholesterol source for steroid hormones

dx: Atypical endometrial hyperplasia in an obese woman with chronic anovulation
case: A 41-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 1 year of irregular, heavy vaginal bleeding. Her cycles vary from 45 to 90 days, and some episodes last 2 weeks. She was diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome at age 22 and has never been pregnant. She takes no hormones. BMI is 42 kg/m2. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 138/86 mm Hg. Examination shows facial hirsutism and acanthosis nigricans of the axillae. Serum hCG is negative. Hemoglobin is 10.1 g/dL (normal 12.0 to 16.0); TSH and prolactin are normal. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows a normal-sized uterus with homogeneous myometrium, an endometrial thickness of 18 mm, and no polyp or fibroid. Endometrial biopsy shows crowded back-to-back glands with nuclear atypia and no stromal invasion. Diagnosis: atypical endometrial hyperplasia.

questions.stem: Immunohistochemistry shows loss of PTEN protein in the atypical glands. Which of the following best explains how this loss promotes growth of the glands?
options: Loss of RB restraint of E2F at the G1 checkpoint
Accumulation of PIP3 with constant AKT signaling
Loss of mismatch repair with microsatellite instability
Failure of p53-mediated arrest after DNA damage
approach: Recall that PTEN is a phosphatase that removes a phosphate from PIP3, turning it back into PIP2.
PIP3 recruits and activates AKT, which promotes cell growth and survival through mTOR.
Without PTEN, PIP3 builds up and AKT stays on, adding to the growth push from unopposed estrogen.
questions.why: PTEN is a tumor suppressor that opposes PI3K by dephosphorylating PIP3. When PTEN is lost, PIP3 accumulates, AKT and mTOR stay active, and cells grow and resist apoptosis. PTEN loss is the most common early molecular change in endometrial hyperplasia and endometrioid carcinoma. Her hyperplasia began with unopposed estrogen from obesity and chronic anovulation, and PTEN loss helps turn that hormonal growth into a clonal, atypical process. Atypical hyperplasia is the direct precursor of endometrioid carcinoma.
whyNot: Loss of RB control of E2F is the mechanism of HPV E7 in cervical neoplasia and of retinoblastoma. It is not the result of PTEN loss.
Correct.
Mismatch repair loss with microsatellite instability is the mechanism in Lynch syndrome. It is a separate pathway from PTEN loss, though both can occur in endometrioid tumors.
Failure of p53-mediated arrest from TP53 mutation is typical of serous endometrial carcinoma, which arises in atrophic endometrium rather than hyperplasia.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the irregular, heavy pattern of her bleeding?
options: Proliferative endometrium breaking down without progesterone
Synchronized shedding of secretory endometrium after luteal regression
Submucosal leiomyoma distorting the endometrial cavity
Endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium
approach: Her long, irregular cycles and PCOS point to chronic anovulation.
Without ovulation, there is no corpus luteum and no progesterone to make the endometrium secretory and stable.
Estrogen keeps thickening a fragile endometrium that outgrows its blood supply and breaks down at random, which is abnormal uterine bleeding from ovulatory dysfunction.
questions.why: In anovulatory cycles, estrogen drives continued proliferation, but no progesterone arrives to convert the endometrium to a stable secretory state. The thick, fragile tissue outgrows its support and breaks down in patches at unpredictable times, so bleeding is irregular, prolonged, and sometimes heavy. In the PALM-COEIN system this is abnormal uterine bleeding from ovulatory dysfunction (formerly called dysfunctional uterine bleeding). Structural causes, such as polyps, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, and malignancy, must be excluded, as her ultrasound and biopsy did here.
whyNot: Correct.
Synchronized shedding after the corpus luteum regresses is a normal ovulatory period, which is regular and predictable.
A submucosal leiomyoma can cause heavy bleeding, but her ultrasound shows no fibroid.
Endometrial tissue within the myometrium is adenomyosis, which gives a large, boggy uterus and painful heavy periods. Her uterus is normal in size with homogeneous myometrium.

topics: Abnormal uterine bleeding from ovulatory dysfunction

questions.stem: Because of her polycystic ovary syndrome, which of the following conditions is she at greatest increased risk of developing?
options: Osteoporosis
Primary ovarian insufficiency
Type 2 diabetes mellitus
Systemic lupus erythematosus
approach: Connect her acanthosis nigricans and obesity to insulin resistance, a core feature of PCOS.
Persistent insulin resistance leads over time to impaired glucose tolerance and type 2 diabetes.
Her estrogen levels are not low, so bone loss is not a main risk.
questions.why: PCOS causes oligomenorrhea, hirsutism, acne, obesity, acanthosis nigricans, and infertility. Insulin resistance is central, so women with PCOS have a much higher risk of impaired glucose tolerance and type 2 diabetes, along with dyslipidemia and metabolic syndrome. Unopposed estrogen raises the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma, as in this patient. Estrogen is preserved and follicles are plentiful, so osteoporosis and early ovarian failure are not expected.
whyNot: Osteoporosis results from low estrogen. Women with PCOS have normal or higher estrogen and are not at increased risk.
Women with PCOS have many follicles and a large follicle reserve, which is the opposite of ovarian insufficiency.
Correct.
PCOS is not linked to systemic lupus erythematosus. Lupus is an autoimmune disease that is more common in women but not tied to PCOS.

questions.stem: Her serum estrone is increased. Which of the following is the main source of this estrogen?
options: Conversion of DHEA sulfate to estrone in the kidney
Direct secretion of estrone by the adrenal cortex
Hepatic synthesis of estrone from cholesterol
Aromatization of androstenedione in adipose tissue
approach: Recall that adipose stromal cells contain aromatase.
Aromatase converts androstenedione from the ovaries and adrenals into estrone.
More fat and more androgen substrate in PCOS mean more estrone, which stimulates the endometrium without progesterone to oppose it.
questions.why: Adipose tissue contains aromatase, which converts androstenedione to estrone and testosterone to estradiol. In obesity, this peripheral conversion becomes a large source of estrogen, especially when ovarian and adrenal androgen output is high, as in PCOS. Without ovulation, there is no progesterone to oppose it, so the endometrium keeps growing and can become hyperplastic. The same process explains gynecomastia in obese men and is the main estrogen source after menopause.
whyNot: The kidney does not convert DHEA sulfate to estrone. DHEA sulfate is an adrenal androgen precursor that can be used for estrogen synthesis in peripheral tissues such as fat.
The adrenal cortex secretes androgen precursors, not significant amounts of estrone.
The liver does not make estrone from cholesterol. It metabolizes and conjugates estrogens.
Correct.

dx: Endometrioid endometrial carcinoma in a woman with Lynch syndrome
case: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 3 months of bleeding between her menstrual periods. At age 43, she had a right colon adenocarcinoma removed. Her father had colon cancer at age 45, and her paternal aunt had endometrial cancer at age 50. She has 2 children. BMI is 25 kg/m2. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows a normal cervix and a normal-sized uterus. Hemoglobin is 11.8 g/dL (normal 12.0 to 16.0). Endometrial biopsy shows a well-differentiated adenocarcinoma with back-to-back glands resembling proliferative endometrium. Immunohistochemistry of the tumor shows loss of MSH2 and MSH6 proteins, and germline testing shows a pathogenic MSH2 mutation. Diagnosis: endometrioid endometrial carcinoma with Lynch syndrome.

questions.stem: Compared with serous carcinoma of the endometrium, her tumor type is characteristically associated with which of the following?
options: Origin in a background of atrophic endometrium
TP53 mutation in nearly all tumor cells
Papillary tufts with psammoma bodies
Origin from endometrial hyperplasia
approach: Identify her tumor as endometrioid: well-differentiated glands that resemble normal endometrium, in a younger woman with Lynch syndrome.
Recall the two-type model: endometrioid carcinoma is estrogen-related and arises from hyperplasia, while serous carcinoma arises in older women with atrophic endometrium.
Match each feature to its tumor type.
questions.why: Endometrioid carcinoma is the more common type. It is driven by estrogen, arises from atypical hyperplasia, and occurs in perimenopausal women with obesity, anovulation, or Lynch syndrome. Its mutations include PTEN, and mismatch repair loss in Lynch syndrome. It is often low grade and has a good prognosis. Serous carcinoma affects older women, arises in atrophic endometrium from a precursor called serous endometrial intraepithelial carcinoma, carries TP53 mutations, and is aggressive. Both types usually present with abnormal or postmenopausal bleeding.
whyNot: Origin in atrophic endometrium is typical of serous carcinoma in older postmenopausal women.
TP53 mutation in nearly all cells is the hallmark of serous carcinoma, not low-grade endometrioid carcinoma.
Papillary architecture with psammoma bodies and marked atypia describes serous carcinoma.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how loss of MSH2 function leads to her cancers?
options: Failure to excise ultraviolet-induced pyrimidine dimers
Failure to correct replication base mismatches
Failure to repair double-strand breaks by recombination
Failure to degrade β-catenin in the WNT pathway
approach: MSH2 and MSH6 are mismatch repair proteins that find mispaired bases left by DNA polymerase.
In Lynch syndrome, one mutant copy is inherited and the second is lost in the tissue, so mismatch repair fails.
Errors pile up, especially in short repeated sequences (microsatellite instability), and hit genes that control growth.
questions.why: Lynch syndrome is caused by germline mutations in mismatch repair genes, mainly MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2. It is autosomal dominant, and tumors form after the second copy is lost. Without mismatch repair, replication errors stay in the DNA, causing microsatellite instability and mutations in growth genes. The syndrome causes colorectal cancer, often right sided, and endometrial cancer, which in affected women is about as common as colon cancer. Ovarian, stomach, small bowel, urinary tract, and biliary cancers are also more frequent.
whyNot: Failure to remove ultraviolet-induced pyrimidine dimers is a nucleotide excision repair defect, as in xeroderma pigmentosum, which causes skin cancers.
Correct.
Failure of homologous recombination repair of double-strand breaks is the defect in BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations, which raise breast and ovarian cancer risk.
Failure to degrade β-catenin results from APC loss in familial adenomatous polyposis, which causes hundreds of colon polyps through chromosomal instability.

topics: DNA repair defects and cancer syndromes

questions.stem: Before the biopsy, her physician considered an endometrial polyp as the cause of her intermenstrual bleeding. Which of the following findings would have characterized a benign endometrial polyp?
options: Localized glands and fibrous stroma with thick-walled vessels
A circumscribed mass of whorled smooth muscle bundles
Benign endometrial glands and stroma deep within the myometrium
Infiltrating glands that invade the endometrial stroma
approach: Picture an endometrial polyp: a sessile or stalked growth that projects into the uterine cavity.
Its structure is a local overgrowth of endometrial glands and a fibrous stroma, with thick-walled blood vessels in the core.
Separate it from leiomyoma (smooth muscle), adenomyosis (glands in myometrium), and carcinoma (invasion).
questions.why: Endometrial polyps are benign, localized overgrowths of endometrial glands and stroma that project into the uterine cavity. Their stroma is often fibrous and contains thick-walled vessels. They cause abnormal or intermenstrual bleeding, and they are more common around menopause and with tamoxifen use. Endocervical polyps are similar growths of the cervical canal that also cause spotting. Polyps rarely turn malignant, but bleeding with a polyp still needs tissue diagnosis, as in this patient.
whyNot: Correct.
Whorled smooth muscle bundles in a circumscribed mass describe a leiomyoma, which arises from the myometrium.
Endometrial glands and stroma deep in the myometrium describe adenomyosis, which enlarges the uterus and causes painful, heavy periods.
Glands that invade the stroma define endometrial carcinoma, not a benign polyp.

topics: Structural causes of abnormal uterine bleeding

questions.stem: Her 58-year-old neighbor, who has no family history of cancer, develops postmenopausal bleeding. Endometrial biopsy shows hyperplasia, and imaging shows a 10-cm solid right ovarian mass. The ovarian tumor has sheets of cells with grooved, coffee-bean nuclei arranged around small spaces filled with eosinophilic material. Serum inhibin is increased. Which of the following best explains the neighbor's endometrial hyperplasia?
options: Testosterone secreted by a Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor
Thyroxine secreted by a struma ovarii
Estradiol secreted by a granulosa cell tumor
hCG secreted by an ovarian choriocarcinoma
approach: Coffee-bean nuclei around small eosinophilic spaces (Call-Exner bodies) and high inhibin identify a granulosa cell tumor.
Granulosa cells have aromatase and make estrogen.
In a postmenopausal woman, that estrogen is unopposed, so it causes endometrial hyperplasia and bleeding.
questions.why: Granulosa cell tumors are sex cord-stromal tumors that make estrogen, and inhibin is a useful tumor marker. Histology shows coffee-bean nuclei with grooves and Call-Exner bodies. In girls, the estrogen causes precocious puberty; in older women, it causes endometrial hyperplasia, bleeding, and sometimes endometrial carcinoma. Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors make androgens and cause virilization. Fibromas make no hormones but can cause Meigs syndrome, with ascites and a right pleural effusion.
whyNot: Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors make androgens and cause hirsutism, clitoromegaly, and voice deepening. They do not cause endometrial hyperplasia.
Struma ovarii is a teratoma made mostly of thyroid tissue and can cause hyperthyroidism, not estrogen excess.
Correct.
Ovarian choriocarcinoma makes hCG and is a germ cell tumor of young women. Its histology is trophoblast, not grooved nuclei around eosinophilic spaces.

dx: Postmenopausal pelvic organ prolapse with cystocele, urethrocele, and rectocele
case: A 68-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a bulge in her vagina and pelvic pressure that worsens through the day. She has a feeling of incomplete bladder emptying, leaks urine when she coughs, and must press on the back wall of her vagina to finish a bowel movement. She has had four vaginal deliveries, one a forceps delivery of a 4.5-kg (9.9-lb) infant. Menopause was at age 51, and she has never taken hormone therapy. She has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with a daily cough. BMI is 31 kg/m2. Pelvic examination with straining shows the anterior vaginal wall bulging to the hymen, descent of the distal anterior wall with urethral hypermobility, a bulging posterior wall, and the cervix descending to the mid-vagina. The vaginal mucosa is thin and pale with loss of rugae. Postvoid residual volume is 180 mL (normal less than 50). Diagnosis: pelvic organ prolapse with cystocele, urethrocele, and rectocele.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how her vaginal deliveries predisposed her to pelvic organ prolapse decades later?
options: Weakening of the transversalis fascia at the deep inguinal ring
Hypertrophy of the detrusor muscle from bladder outlet obstruction
Stretch injury of the levator ani and its nerve supply
Separation of the rectus abdominis muscles along the linea alba
approach: Recall that the pelvic organs are held up by the levator ani and by connective tissue (endopelvic fascia and its ligaments).
A large baby and forceps stretch and tear the levator ani and stretch the pudendal nerve and the nerves to the levator ani.
Later, estrogen loss, aging, obesity, and chronic cough add strain to the damaged support, and the organs herniate into the vagina.
questions.why: Cystocele, urethrocele, and rectocele are hernias of pelvic organs through weakened pelvic floor muscle and endopelvic fascia. Vaginal childbirth is the main risk factor, especially with large babies, forceps, and many deliveries, because it stretches or tears the levator ani and injures its nerves. Aging and estrogen loss weaken connective tissue. Obesity, chronic cough, and chronic straining raise abdominal pressure that pushes the organs down. She has all of these risks.
whyNot: Weakness of the transversalis fascia at the deep inguinal ring leads to an indirect inguinal hernia, not to vaginal wall prolapse.
Detrusor hypertrophy follows bladder outlet obstruction, as in benign prostatic hyperplasia. Childbirth does not cause it, and it does not cause prolapse.
Correct.
Separation of the rectus muscles (diastasis recti) affects the anterior abdominal wall after pregnancy. It does not support the pelvic organs.

topics: Risk factors for pelvic organ prolapse

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why she must press on the back wall of her vagina to complete defecation?
options: Rectum bulging into the posterior vaginal wall
Bladder bulging into the anterior vaginal wall
Urethra descending with the distal anterior wall
Cervix descending along the axis of the vagina
approach: Match each symptom to the wall that bulges: anterior wall for bladder and urethra, posterior wall for rectum.
When the rectum bulges into the posterior vaginal wall, stool pushes into the pouch instead of out of the anus.
Pressing on the posterior vaginal wall (splinting) straightens the path so stool can pass.
questions.why: A rectocele is herniation of the rectum through a weak rectovaginal septum into the posterior vaginal wall. Stool collects in the pouch, so emptying is hard and many women splint the vagina or perineum to finish. A cystocele is the bladder bulging into the upper anterior wall and causes incomplete emptying and a high postvoid residual, as she has. A urethrocele is the urethra descending with the lower anterior wall and causes stress incontinence with coughing.
whyNot: Correct.
A bladder bulging into the anterior wall is a cystocele. It explains her incomplete bladder emptying and high postvoid residual, not her trouble with defecation.
Urethral descent with the lower anterior wall is a urethrocele. It explains her leaking with coughing.
Cervical descent is uterine prolapse, which causes a sense of pressure and a bulge but does not trap stool.

questions.stem: Weakening of which of the following structures most directly allows her cervix to descend into the vagina?
options: Round ligament of the uterus
Broad ligament
Ovarian ligament
Cardinal ligament
approach: Cervical descent is uterine prolapse, a failure of support at the top of the vagina.
The cervix and upper vagina are held by the cardinal (transverse cervical) and uterosacral ligaments, resting on the levator ani and perineal body below.
The round, broad, and ovarian ligaments hold position or carry vessels but give little support against descent.
questions.why: The uterus and upper vagina are held up by condensations of endopelvic fascia, mainly the cardinal ligaments, which run from the cervix and lateral vaginal fornix to the lateral pelvic wall and contain the uterine vessels, and the uterosacral ligaments, which run to the sacrum. Below, the levator ani and perineal body form the floor. When these supports weaken, the cervix and uterus slide down the vagina. Childbirth injury, aging, and estrogen loss all contribute.
whyNot: The round ligament runs from the uterine horn through the inguinal canal to the labium majus. It helps keep the uterus tipped forward but does not prevent descent.
The broad ligament is a peritoneal fold over the uterus, tubes, and ovaries. It carries vessels and gives little support against descent.
The ovarian ligament connects the ovary to the uterus. It holds the ovary in place but does not support the cervix.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her serum FSH is 82 mIU/mL (follicular phase reference 3.5 to 12.5). Which of the following best explains this elevation?
options: Gonadotroph hyperplasia driven by rising adrenal androgens
Reduced renal clearance of FSH with aging
Loss of ovarian inhibin and estradiol feedback
Increased hypothalamic GnRH release from falling prolactin
approach: Menopause is the depletion of ovarian follicles.
Granulosa cells of those follicles make inhibin and estradiol, which hold FSH and LH down.
With no follicles, feedback is lost and FSH rises most, followed by LH. The same estrogen loss explains her thin, pale vaginal mucosa.
questions.why: Menopause happens when the ovarian follicle pool runs out. Without follicles, the ovary stops making inhibin and estradiol, so negative feedback ends and FSH and LH rise, with FSH rising earlier and higher. Estrogen loss causes vasomotor symptoms, atrophic vaginitis with thin pale mucosa and loss of rugae, bone loss and osteoporosis, and higher cardiovascular risk. It also weakens pelvic connective tissue, which adds to her prolapse.
whyNot: Adrenal androgens fall with age, and they do not cause gonadotroph hyperplasia.
FSH levels rise from more secretion, not from slower clearance. Renal clearance changes do not explain this large rise.
Correct.
Prolactin changes do not drive the rise in FSH after menopause. The main cause is lost ovarian feedback.
